The experiments were conducted in the Allison Aerothermodynamic Cascade Facility, which can simulate a wide range of engine operating conditions.
The test vane had a total of 123 surface thermocouples and 46 surface static pressure taps, with 11 redundant thermocouples and pressure taps.
The leading edge film cooling array had 5 rows of holes with a hole diameter of 0.099 cm (0.039 in) and a length-to-diameter ratio of 3.35.
The downstream film cooling arrays on the suction and pressure surfaces each had 2 rows of holes with the same hole diameter and length-to-diameter ratio as the leading edge.
The coolant flow rates to each of the three film cooling arrays were independently controlled and measured using calibrated orifice meters.

Heat transfer coefficients for the 10 internal radial cooling holes were calculated from the hole diameter, coolant flow rate, and coolant temperature, with a correction for thermal entry region effects.
The vane was fabricated in two pieces, with the film cooled leading edge section thermally isolated from the rest of the vane by a sealed air gap.
The exit Mach numbers tested were 0.75 and 0.90, with a true chord Reynolds number on the order of 10^6.
The coolant-to-gas temperature ratio and coolant-to-gas pressure ratio were varied to study the effects on heat transfer.
Cascade throat static pressures were measured using seven-element pressure rakes installed in grooves on the pressure and suction surfaces.
The data from this study extend the database generated in previous studies on non-film cooled and leading edge film cooled turbine vanes.
The results show that downstream film cooling can provide significant cooling benefits, but the process is complex due to competing thermal dilution and turbulence augmentation effects.
The data and analysis from this study are intended to help improve heat transfer design capabilities for film cooled turbine airfoils.
The C3X vane profile used in this study was the same as in previous studies, allowing the data to be directly compared.
The redundant thermocouples and pressure taps were used to verify the two-dimensionality of the heat transfer and pressure measurements.
